ourAnswer: Cannot represent a travelling wave - 1/(x + vt) diverges at x = -vt
keyAnswer: Only function (c) satisfies the condition [i.e. (c) CAN represent a travelling wave]
note: THE KEY CONTRADICTS ITS OWN STATED CRITERION, which is the whole evidence here and needs no computation. Its sentence is: 'An obvious requirement for an acceptable function for a travelling wave is that it should be finite everywhere and at all times. Only function (c) satisfies this condition.' But 1/(x + vt) is NOT finite everywhere: at the point x = -vt it diverges, and such a point exists at every instant t (at t = 0 it is x = 0). So (c) fails the very test the key names one sentence earlier. A charitable reading is that NCERT means 'finite as x -> +/- infinity', which (c) alone satisfies while (a) and (b) blow up there - but that is not the criterion the key states, and an infinite displacement of the medium is unphysical wherever it occurs. Recorded as a key error rather than a book-internal inconsistency because the key makes a definite verdict that its own test refutes. Flagging honestly: this is a long-contested item and many teachers follow the key; the maintainer may prefer to preserve it as a printed defect with both readings recorded.

THE STRONGEST EVIDENCE IS THAT THE KEY CONTRADICTS ITSELF ACROSS PARTS OF THE SAME QUESTION. With lambda = 125 cm the rule is delta-phi = 2 pi (delta-x / lambda), which gives 6.4 pi for delta-x = 4 m and 3 pi / 2 for delta-x = 3 lambda / 4. TWO mechanisms each reproduce the printed pi/2 exactly and the evidence does not distinguish them, so neither is asserted: (i) reducing 3 pi / 2 to the smallest equivalent phase difference, or (ii) computing for lambda/4 instead of 3 lambda / 4.
